4. C Memory Management

4.1. Overview

A process has 4 separate regions in memory, each with their own rules. Each process gets its own virtual address space that starts at 0x0…0 and is interpreted using that process’s page tables. Stack = local variables, parameters, and return addresses.

Memory SegmentContentsMemory Management
StackLocal variables, parameters, and return addressesAutomatic; grows downward
HeapDynamically allocated storageResizes on demand (e.g. malloc to allocate storage, free to free storage); grows upward
Data (aka Static)Global variablesSize is fixed (“static”) throughout the whole program, preallocated OS loader at program start based on what compiler+linker put in the executable.
Text (aka Code)Program codeSize is fixed throughout the whole program; data is loaded when program starts

The heap let’s you (manually) store memory whose lifetime is not tied to a single function. E.g. you can create something in the heap in a function and pass a pointer to it (see safe example 2 below).

Remark. Python runs on top of the same OS process model but uses stack and heaps differently. For example objects mostly live on the heap. See 6.1010

4.2. Stack

The stack is organized into frames which have their own local variables. It can global variables in the Data but cannot access frames above it. It includes space for the following:

  1. Local variables declared within the function
  2. A return address, i.e. the instruction address in th etext segment that should be next accessed after this function finishes execution.
  3. functions argument

Some properties

  • Allocation and deallocation is fast thanks to the stack pointer which tells us the address of the top of the stack (bottom in diagram above). The compiler knows how much to allocate/deallocate.
    • The stack pointer itself must live somewhere. Instead of living in memory, it lives on the CPU in a special hardware register, so that it can be read and updated quickly. This is a detail we handwave for now and discuss in detail later.
  • When a function returns and the stack pointer moves up, the system does not erase the memory. There is “no time” to zero it out; C is too busy. Memory lower in the stack is overwritten when other functions are called.

  • It is catastrophic to return pointers for the above reason, as it may get overriden. Should return value instead.

Example: square elements in array

Unsafe example

#include <stddef.h>

int* square_unsafe(const int* a, size_t n) {
    int out[1024];                 // stack-allocated (dies when function returns)
    if (n > 1024) n = 1024;
    for (size_t i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        out[i] = a[i] * a[i];
    }
    return out;                    // UNSAFE: returns pointer to dead stack memory
}

Safe version 1 (caller provides the output buffer; no ownership confusion)

#include <stddef.h>

void square_into(int* out, const int* a, size_t n) {
    for (size_t i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        out[i] = a[i] * a[i];
    }
}

/* usage:
   int in[] = {1,2,3};
   int out[3];
   square_into(out, in, 3);
*/

Safe version 2 (function allocates on heap)

#include <stddef.h>
#include <stdlib.h>

int* square_heap(const int* a, size_t n) {
    int* out = (int*)malloc(n * sizeof(int));
    if (!out) return NULL;
    for (size_t i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        out[i] = a[i] * a[i];
    }
    return out;                    // SAFE: heap memory outlives the function
}

/* usage:
   int in[] = {1,2,3};
   int* out = square_heap(in, 3);
   if (out) { ...; free(out); }
*/

4.3. Heap

Recall we treat memory as a long grid of bytes, each with an address and a value (Section 3.2)

Memory on the heap (not actually a heap) is managed with standard C library functions in stdlib. Recall size_tis an unsigned integer type big enough to count memory bytes.

  1. void *malloc(size_t n): memory allococation, i.e. allocate a memory block on the heap.
    1. void * means it returns a generic pointer.
    2. Returns NULL if there is no available contiguous block.
    3. Many C programmers prefer to use calloc as it initializes all bits in the allocated block to zero.
  2. void free(void *ptr): free memory on the heap, input the pointer returned by malloc/realloc
  3. void *realloc(void *ptr, size_t size): reallocate a previously allocated block to a larger/smaller memory block on the heap.
    1. Returns NULL if there is no available contiguous block.

Properties

  • This bookkeeping system can be implemented under the hood via a circular linked list of all free blocks ([TODO] think about algorithms).

  • This differs from the stack (size of frame predetermined) in that we need not know the sizes of memory blocks on the heap at compile-time.
  • The heap is typically much larger than the stack, and the memory blocks are not necessarily allocated in contiguous order.
  • A single request will return a contiguous block of memory. Back-to-back heap requests can fragment the blocks.

4.4. Words, Endianness

A hardware word is a unit of data that determines the smallest(or most efficiently) accessible unit of memory. E.g. 32-bit architecture has a word size of 32-bits.

Pointers are often one word. This relates to above discussion on how for a 32-bit architecture, a pointer can address 4GB in memory.

Instead of visualizing memory as one long line, we view memory as rows of 4 bytes:

Addresses in the left colun are multiples of 4 and hence words.

When data occupies multiple contiguous bytes in memory, we must determine which of the bytes is stored at the lowest address. Little endian stores least significant byte first at the lowest address. Big endian stores most significant byte.
